ZAANAIM*
KJV spelling of Tsa’ananim (Zaanannim) in Judges 4:11. See Zaanannim.
ZAANAN

Village mentioned in Mikah’s (Micah’s) lament over Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Mi 1:11). Tsa’anan (Zaanan) is probably a play on the Hebrew word yatsa’, “to come forth.” The village was in the Shefelah (Shephelah); it is probably the same place as Tsenan (Zenan).
See also Zenan.
ZAANANNIM

One of the markers of the border of Naftali (Naphtali) listed between Helef (Heleph) and Adami-Nekev (Adami-nekeb) (Jos 19:33). Judges 4:11 puts it near Kedesh. There Sisera took refuge in the tent of Hever (Heber) the Keyni (Kenite) and was killed by Ya’el (Jael) (vv 11-21). While the precise location is not known, it was west of Lake el-Huleh (modern Merom) in a region that was probably marshy in ancient times. Though the kjv translates the text as “plain of Zaanaim,” it is more likely “Oak of Tsa’ananim (Zaanannim)” (rsv, niv, nlt). Since many terebinth trees are located in the region, the text is probably referring to a terebinth set aside as a sacred tree.
ZAAVAN
Second son of Ezer, a Hori (Horite) clan chief (Gn 36:27; 1 Chr 1:42).
ZABAD
1. Son of Natan (Nathan) (1 Chr 2:36) and a descendant of Ahlay (Ahlai) the daughter of Sheshan (vv 30, 34-36).
2. Tahat’s (Tahath’s) son and the father of Shutelah (Shuthelah) from Efrayim’s (Ephraim’s) tribe (1 Chr 7:21).
3. One of David’s mighty men, listed as a son of Ahlay (1 Chr 11:41); he is perhaps the same as #1 above.

4. One of the assassins of King Yoash (Joash), listed as the son of Shim’at (Shimeath) the Amonit (Ammonitess) (2 Chr 24:26). He is identical to Yozakar (Jozacar) (alternately “Yozavad (Jozabad)”) in 2 Kings 12:21. Zavad (Zabad) was a palace official who was likely the agent of a powerful conspiracy against Yoash.
See also Jozacar, Jozachar.
5–7. Three priests variously descended from Zatu (Zattu), Hashum, and Nevo (Nebo), who renounced their foreign wives at Ezra’s request during the postexilic period (Ezr 10:27, 33, 43).
ZABBAI
1. Bevay’s (Bebai’s) son and one of the priests who divorced his foreign wife at Ezra’s command (Ezr 10:28).
2. Father of Baruk (Baruch). Baruk repaired a section of the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall during Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) day (Neh 3:20).
ZABBUD*
KJV form of Zakur (Zaccur), Bigvay’s (Bigvai’s) descendant, in Ezra 8:14. See Zaccur #5.
ZABDI
1. Zerah’s descendant from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (Jos 7:1). Akan (Achan) was a Zarhi (Zerahite) of the family of Zavdi (Zabdi) (Jos 7:17-18); alternately called Zimri (nlt mg, 1 Chr 2:6).
2. Shimei’s son and a descendant of Ehud from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:19).
3. David’s officer over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars (1 Chr 27:27). He is called a Shifmi (Shiphmite), which likely means that he was a native of Shefam (Shepham).
4. One of the temple musicians of the order of Asaf (Asaph) (Neh 11:17); alternately called Zicri (1 Chr 9:15).
ZABDIEL
1. Father of Yashaveam (Jashobeam), the commander of the first division of David’s army (1 Chr 27:2).
2. Priest and overseer of 128 “mighty men of valor” (rsv, Neh 11:14). The notation that he was a “son of Haggedolim” might indicate that he was a “son of the mighty men.”
3. Aravi (Arab) who beheaded Alexandros (Alexander) (Balas) Epifanes (Epiphanes) and sent the head to Ptolemaios (Ptolemy) (1 Macc 11:17).
ZABUD

Priest in Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) court and the “king’s friend” (1 Kgs 4:5). The phrase “king’s friend” may be an official title given to one of the king’s advisers. Hushay (Hushai) the Arki (Archite) had a similar title in David’s court (2 Sm 15:37; 16:16).
ZABULON*
KJV spelling of Zevulun (Zebulun) in Matthew 4:13-15 and Revelation 7:8. See Zebulun, Tribe of.
ZACCAI
Forefather of a family who returned with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) to Yehudah (Judah) following the exile (Ezr 2:9; Neh 7:14).
ZACCHAEUS

Jewish tax collector who collected taxes for the Romans at Yeriho (Jericho). He probably secured this position by purchasing the exclusive right to collect revenue in that region or by working as a subcontractor for another affluent official. In either case, Zakay (Zacchaeus; Grk. Zakkaios) himself accrued great wealth (largely by illegitimate means) from his customs enterprise. Yeriho, a significant center of commerce, was situated along a major trade route connecting Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and its environs with the lands east of the Yarden (Jordan).

In his Gospel, Lukas (Luke) records Zakay’s encounter with Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Lk 19:2-8). Seeking Yeshua, but unable to see him over the crowd because of his small stature, Zakay climbed a sycamore tree to get a better view when Yeshua passed by. To his astonishment, Yeshua stopped under the tree and after calling him down, invited himself to the publican’s house for the night. Subsequently, Zakay repented and followed Yeshua, promising to restore fourfold to those whom he had wrongfully exploited and give to the poor. According to Clement of Alexandria, Zakay later became the bishop of Kaisareia (Caesarea) (Homily 3.63).
ZACCHUR*
KJV spelling of Zakur (Zaccur), Hamuel’s (Hammuel’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 4:26. See Zaccur #2.
ZACCUR
1. Re’uveni (Reubenite) and father of Shamua (Shammua), one of the 12 spies in the reconnaissance of Kena’an (Canaan) (Nm 13:4).
2. Shim’oni (Simeonite) who was the son of Hamuel (Hammuel) and the father of Shimei (1 Chr 4:26).
3. One of the descendants of Merari in the record of the divisions of the priests (1 Chr 24:27).

4. One of the sons of Asaf (Asaph) who was assigned responsibility for the temple service (1 Chr 25:2). Zakur (Zaccur) and his sons and brothers were assigned the third lot among the various duties for the temple musicians (1 Chr 25:10). Descendants of Zakur were present at the dedication of the city wall following the exile (Neh 12:35).
5. One of the descendants of Bigvay (Bigvai) who returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with Ezra (Ezr 8:14).
6. Son of Imri who worked on repairing Yerushalem’s wall in the vicinity of the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:2).
7. One of the Levites who signed Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) covenant to obey the law of God (Neh 10:12).
8. Son of Matanyah (Mattaniah) and father of Hanan, the assistant to the storehouse treasurers during Nehemyah’s time (Neh 13:13). Some have suggested that he is the same as #7 above.
ZACHARIAH*
1. KJV spelling of Zekaryah (Zechariah), king of Yisrael (Israel), in 2 Kings 14:29 and 15:8, 11. See Zechariah (Person) #1.
2. KJV spelling of Zekaryah, King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) maternal grandfather, in 2 Kings 18:2. See Zechariah (Person) #2.
ZACHARIAS*
1. KJV spelling of Zekaryah (Zechariah), Yehoyada’s (Jehoiada’s) son, in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51. See Zechariah (Person) #14.
2. KJV spelling of Zekaryah, Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser’s father, in Luke 1:5-67. See Zechariah (Person) #31.
3. KJV spelling of Zekaryah, a proposed name for Yohan the immerser, in Luke 1:59. See John the Baptist; Zechariah (Person) #32.
ZACHER*
KJV form of Zekaryah (Zechariah), or Zeker, in 1 Chronicles 8:31. See Zechariah (Person) #5.
ZADOK
Common OT name meaning “righteous one.”

1. David’s priest, probably the most famous and influential of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) high priests apart from Aharon (Aaron). He first appeared at the time of Avshalom’s (Absalom’s) revolt, when he and his fellow priest Evyatar (Abiathar) showed their loyalty to David by coming to him with the ark, fully prepared to share his exile (2 Sm 15:24-29). David refused their offer and sent them back to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to act in his interests.

In 2 Samuel 8:17, Tsadok (Zadok) is listed as the son of Ahituv (Ahitub), who is noted in 1 Samuel 14:3 as the grandson of Eli. In the genealogies of Chronicles, Tsadok’s descent through Ahituv is traced back to Eleazar, the eldest son of Aharon (1 Chr 6:1-8, 50-53; Ezr 7:2-5), but with no reference to Eli. A slight problem emerges in that Tsadok replaces the banished Evyatar, a descendant of Eli. This is regarded as the fulfillment of an earlier prophecy that the tenure of the high priestly office by Eli’s family would be broken in favor of a different branch of Aharon’s family (1 Sm 2:30-36; 1 Kgs 2:26-27).

In both summaries of David’s court officials (2 Sm 8:17; 20:25), Tsadok is listed as one of David’s two principal priests, an office held throughout the latter part of David’s reign. When David was near death, a power struggle over the throne was precipitated by Adoniyah (Adonijah), David’s oldest surviving son. With the support of Yoav (Joab), the commander of the army, and the priest Evyatar, David’s long-standing friend, Adoniyah declared himself king (1 Kgs 1:5-10). Natan (Nathan) the prophet promptly intervened with Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba) as Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) advocate. Tsadok and Benayah (Benaiah), the captain of the mercenary troops, supported Shelomoh. Adoniyah’s cause was hopeless once David had indicated his approval of Natan’s plans. Consequently, the discredited Evyatar was banished (2:26-27), leaving the loyal Tsadok as Shelomoh’s chief priest (2:35; 4:4).

In the centuries that followed, the descendants of Tsadok preserved this dominance, and as Yerushalem’s prestige increased, so did their status. Azaryah (Azariah), the chief priest in Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) reign, was a Zadokite (2 Chr 31:10). Yehezkel (Ezekiel) restricted the main priestly functions to the “sons of Tsadok,” demoting the Levites generally to the rank of “temple caretakers” because of their apostasy during the monarchy (Ez 44:10-16). When the Yehudim (Jews) came under Seleucid domination in the early second century BC, the high priesthood, regarded as a political appointment, was taken away from the Zadokites. Conservative elements, however, like the Qumran covenanters, continued to look for its restoration.
See also David; Israel, History of.
2. Father-in-law of Uziyah (Uzziah) and grandfather of Yotam (Jotham), kings of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Kgs 15:32-33; 2 Chr 27:1).
3. Descendant of Tsadok, David’s priest (1 Chr 6:12; 9:11; Neh 11:11).
4. Young man of exceptional courage, the leader of a contingent that joined David at Hevron (Hebron) against Sha’ul (Saul) (1 Chr 12:28).
5. Son of Ba’ana (Baana), who helped to repair the wall of Yerushalem in Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) time (Neh 3:4).
6. Son of Imer (Immer), who also shared in Nehemyah’s rebuilding operations (Neh 3:29).
7. Signatory to Nehemyah’s covenant (Neh 10:21) and perhaps identifiable with #5 or #6 above.
8. One of three treasurers appointed by Nehemyah during his second term of office, called the scribe (Neh 13:13).
9. Ancestor of Christ (Mt 1:14). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
ZAHAM
One of Rehav’am’s (Rehoboam’s) sons by his wife Mahalat (Mahalath) (2 Chr 11:19).
ZAIR

Place where Yoram (Joram) attacked and defeated the Edomim (Edomites) (2 Kgs 8:21). In the parallel passage of 2 Chronicles 21:9, the phrase “to Tsa’ir (Zair)” is replaced by the phrase “with his commanders” (the Hebrew words are similar). Many have therefore suggested that a copyist revision appeared in 2 Chronicles because the location of Tsa’ir was unknown. Others have suggested that Tsa’ir should be identified with Tsoar (Zoar) on the southeast end of the Dead Sea, or with Se’ir (Seir) in Edom. In any case, it was located in Transjordan on a principal road to Edom.
ZALAPH
Hanun’s father. Hanun repaired a section of the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall during Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) day (Neh 3:30).
ZALMON (Person)
One of David’s mighty men (2 Sm 23:28); alternately called Ilay (Ilai) the Ahohi (Ahohite) in 1 Chronicles 11:29.
ZALMON (Place)

Mountain from which Avimelek (Abimelech) took brush to burn down the tower of Shekem (Shechem) (Jgs 9:48). Since the mountain obviously was close to Shekem, it tentatively has been identified with es-Sulemiyeh (the modern name for the southeastern portion of Mt Eyval (Ebal)) or one of its surrounding hills. Tsalmon (Zalmon) is also mentioned in connection with the defeat of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) enemies in Psalm 68:14. Because of the mention of snowfall and the “mighty mountain of Bashan” in the following verse, the Septuagint and some commentators consider this Tsalmon to be Mt Hermon in Levanon (Lebanon). However, seasonal snowfalls also occur in the region of Mt Eyval.
ZALMONAH
Place where the Israelis (Israelites) camped after they set out from Mt Hor (Nm 33:41-42). The name suggests that it was a gloomy valley leading up to the Edomi (Edomite) plateau.
ZALMUNNA
See Zebah and Zalmunna.
ZAMZUMMIM*, ZAMZUMMITES

Amoni (Ammonite) name for the Refaim (Rephaim), who are described as a “people great and many, and tall as the Anakim” (Dt 2:20). The Zamzumim (Zamzummites) were displaced by the Amonim (Ammonites), just as the Horim (Horites) were displaced by the Edomim (Edomites) and the Avim (Avvim) by the Kaftorim (Caphtorim). The comparison with the Anakim, the Refaim, and the Emim makes it evident that the Zamzumim were a race of giants who lived in Transjordan. While their precise origin is unknown, they probably resided in the vicinity of Rabbath-ammon.
See also Giants; Rephaim.
ZANOAH (Person)

Descendant of Kalev (Caleb) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:18). Zanoah was the son of Yekutiel (Jekuthiel) and, depending on the translation of the Hebrew text, may have been related to Bityah (Bithiah), the daughter of Par’oh (Pharaoh). Some have interpreted the text as indicating that Yekutiel was the founder or principal settler of the city named Zanoah. In any case, Zanoah’s descendants may well have been connected with the city of that name.
ZANOAH (Place)

1. One of the cities “in the lowland” that was part of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) inheritance (Jos 15:34). The inhabitants of Zanoah worked with Hanun to rebuild the Valley Gate as well as about 1,500 feet (457.2 meters) of the city wall during the restoration of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Neh 3:13; 11:30). The city is probably identifiable with Zanu’a, which is located approximately 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) west of Yerushalem.

2. One of the cities in the Yehudi (Judean) highlands south of Hevron (Hebron) that was part of Yehudah’s inheritance (Jos 15:56). It was probably inhabited by the descendants of Zanoah, Yekutiel’s (Jekuthiel’s) son.
ZAPHENATH-PANEAH

Name given to Yosef (Joseph) by Par’oh (Pharaoh) when Yosef assumed his governmental responsibilities in Mitsrayim (Egypt) (Gn 41:45). The name most likely means “says the god, he will live.” See Joseph #1.
ZAPHON

Town located east of the Yarden (Jordan) River (Jos 13:27) and included as part of the inheritance of Gad’s tribe (v 24). Mitsri (Egyptian) records (13th century BC) refer to a town known as Dapuna, while an Amarna text spells the name Sapuna.
ZARA*, ZARAH*
KJV alternate forms of Zerah, Yehudah’s (Judah’s) son, in Genesis 38:30, 46:12, and Matthew 1:3. See Zerah #2.
ZAREAH*, ZAREATHITE*
KJV spelling of Tsor’ah (Zorah) and Tsor’ati (Zorathite) in Nehemiah 11:29 and 1 Chronicles 2:53, respectively. See Zorah, Zorathite.
ZARED*
KJV spelling for the valley of Zered in Numbers 21:12. See Zered.
ZAREPHATH

Village where the woman who provided food and lodging for Eliyah (Elijah) lived (1 Kgs 17:9-10; Lk 4:26). Ovadyah (Obadiah) later prophesied that the Israeli (Israelite) exiles of Halah would “possess Foinikai (Phoenicia) as far as Tserefat (Zarephath)” (Ob 1:20). Tserefat was under the control of Tsidon (Sidon) at the time Eliyah visited, thus serving as a safe haven from King Ahav (Ahab) of Yisrael (Israel). Tserefat is likely identifiable with modern Surafend, where a chapel marks the traditional site for the widow’s house.
ZARETHAN

City or region near the Yarden (Jordan) River north of Yeriho (Jericho). It is first mentioned in connection with the “cutting off” of the waters of the Yarden that occurred at Adam, “the city that is beside Tseretan (Zarethan)” (Jos 3:16). Its location is more precisely defined in the list of Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) administrative districts as being in the vicinity of Beth-shan below Yizre’el (Jezreel) (1 Kgs 4:12). Bronze utensils for Shelomoh’s temple were cast near there (7:46; 2 Chr 4:17, “Tseredah (Zeredah)”).
ZARETH-SHAHAR*
KJV spelling of Tseret-Hashahar (Zereth-shahar), a Re’uveni (Reubenite) city, in Joshua 13:19. See Zereth-shahar.
ZARHITE*
1. KJV spelling of Zarhi (Zerahite), a descendant of Zerah’s family in Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) tribe, in Numbers 26:13. See Zerah #3.
2. KJV spelling of Zarhi, a descendant of Zerah’s family in Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe, in Numbers 26:20. See Zerah #2.
ZARTANAH*, ZARTHAN*
KJV alternate forms of Tseretan (Zarethan) in 1 Kings 4:12 and 7:46, respectively. See Zarethan.
ZATTHU*
KJV rendering of Zatu (Zattu) in Nehemiah 10:14. See Zattu #2.
ZATTU

1. Clan chief with whom 945 people returned with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) (Ezr 2:8; Neh 7:13 cites 845 returnees). Of the priests who renounced their foreign wives, six are listed as “sons” of Zatu (Zattu) (Ezr 10:27).
2. One of the chiefs of the people who signed Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) covenant (Neh 10:14); perhaps the same person as #1 above.
ZAVAN*
KJV spelling of Za’avan (Zaavan), Ezer’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:42. See Zaavan.
ZAZA
Yonatan’s (Jonathan’s) son, in the family of Yerahme’el (Jerahmeel), a member of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:33).
ZEALOT

Term used for the second Shim’on (Simon) among the Twelve to distinguish him from Shim’on Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) (Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13). Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) (Mt 10:4) and Markos (Mark) (Mk 3:18) use “Cananaean”—Greek and Aramaic equivalents for “zealous defender, enthusiast, one eager to acquire, fanatic” (from root words meaning “burn with zeal, or jealousy; desire eagerly”; Ex 34:14; 2 Macc 4:2). In this general sense, Christ showed zeal for God’s house. Some were “zealots” for spiritual gifts, good works, goodness, and the law, as Paulos (Paul) was for the tradition of the fathers and for God (Jn 2:17; Acts 21:20; 22:3; 1 Cor 14:12; Gal 1:14; Ti 2:14). So, Shim’on was distinguished from Kefa and the others by his religious zeal.

By the time Lukas (Luke) wrote, the title “Zealot” had become attached especially to a militant, anti-Roman, revolutionary faction, equally religious and political in motivation. This party may have been founded in AD 6, following the death of Herodes (Herod) the Great, by Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) the Galili (Galilean) and Zadduk the Pharisee. The movement was rooted in Maccabean resistance to foreign rule and infiltration (1 Macc 2:15-28). Zealot opposition to Roman rule was rooted in zeal for the Torah and for God the only King. The Zealot regarded himself as an agent of divine judgment and redemption, resolutely and fearlessly contending against idolatry, apostasy, and collaboration. The Zealots thought that the Messiah would become their leader.

As hostility between Romai (Rome) and Judea sharpened, the religious motivation was channeled by nationalist feeling into a “holy war.” Whereas the Maccabees had been forced to take arms in self-defense, the Zealots became increasingly militaristic. Josephus (Antiquities 18.1.1-6; War 4.3.9), with some prejudice, calls them brigands and robbers. Their Latin name was sicarii, assassins, but supporters would call them patriotic guerrillas. They reached preeminence in the revolt against Romai (AD 66–70). Their last refuge and stronghold, at Masada, was overcome in AD 73, when the surviving 960 committed suicide.

Shim’on probably was, or had been, a member of this movement’s earlier phase, around AD 30. It is less probable that Yehudah Iskariot (Iscariot) (possibly Sicarius) and the “sons of thunder” (Mk 3:17) were. Yehudah the Galili (Acts 5:37-38), and even Paulos (21:38), were considered Zealots.
See also First Jewish Revolt; Judaism.
ZEALOT, Shim’on (Simon) the
See Simon #5.
ZEBADIAH
1. One of the sons of Beriah from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:15).
2. One of the sons of Elpa’al (Elpaal) from Benyamin’s tribe (1 Chr 8:17).
3. One of the sons of Yeroham (Jeroham) of Gedor, who came to David’s support at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:7).
4. Korhi (Korahite) Levite descended from Asaf (Asaph), third of Meshelemyah’s (Meshelemiah’s) seven sons and a temple gatekeeper (1 Chr 26:2).
5. Son of Asahel, Yoav’s (Joab’s) brother, who was the commander of the fourth division of David’s army (1 Chr 27:7).
6. One of the Levites sent by Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) into the cities of Yehudah (Judah) to teach the law (2 Chr 17:8).
7. Yishmael’s (Ishmael’s) son and one of the leaders of the Levites whom Yehoshafat appointed as governor of civil affairs for the house of Yehudah (2 Chr 19:11).
8. Mika’el’s (Michael’s) son from Shefatyah’s (Shephatiah’s) house, who returned with Ezra to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) following the exile (Ezr 8:8).
9. One of the sons of Imer (Immer) who renounced his foreign wife at Ezra’s command (Ezr 10:20).
ZEBAH AND ZALMUNNA
Two Midyanite (Midianite) kings who slaughtered Gid’on’s (Gideon’s) brothers at Tavor (Tabor). Gid’on subsequently killed them in order to avenge his brothers’ deaths (Jgs 8:18-21).

During Gid’on’s day, Midyanite camel raiders annually made forays into Israeli (Israelite) territory at harvesttime, stealing crops and livestock (Jgs 6:3). So complete were their raids that nothing was left in Yisrael (Israel), including crops, sheep, oxen, or donkeys.

In this state of affairs God called Gid’on to deliver Yisrael (Jgs 6:16). His well-known victory over Midyan (Midian) near Mt Moreh was an important step toward realization of this divine commission (7:1-23). In the operations following the battle, Efrati (Ephraimite) warriors captured and assassinated two Midyanite leaders named Ze’ev (Zeeb) and Orev (Oreb) (7:24–8:3).

Gid’on determined to capture Zevah (Zebah) and Tsalmuna (Zalmunna), the kings of the Midyanite forces. In tracking them down, he crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River and traveled more than 100 miles (160.9 kilometers) from the site of the original battle. Along the way, two successive towns, Sukot (Succoth) and Penuel, refused to help Gid’on and his men, doubtless fearing reprisal from the Midyanite raiders should Gid’on fail to defeat them.

Gid’on routed the remaining Midyanite warriors and captured Zevah and Tsalmuna (Jgs 8:12). Because Zevah and Tsalmuna had killed his brothers, Gid’on killed the two Midyanite kings (vv 19-21). Psalm 83:11 indicates that Zevah, Tsalmuna, and the Midyanites (Midianites) were the enemies not merely of Yisrael but also of God.
ZEBAIM*
KJV rendering of a place mentioned in Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59. See Pochereth-Hazzebaim, Pochereth of Zebaim.
ZEBEDEE

Father of the disciples Ya’akov (James) and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) (Mt 26:37; Mk 3:17; 10:35). Zavday (Zebedee) was in the fishing business and may have been wealthy, considering that he had servants and apparent connections with the high priest (Jn 18:15). Although he personally appears only once in the narrative (Mt 4:21; Mk 1:19-20), his wife, Salome, appears frequently as one of the pious women who followed Christ.
ZEBIDAH
Mother of Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim), king of Yehudah (Judah), Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) wife and the daughter of Pedayah (Pedaiah) (2 Kgs 23:36).
ZEBINA
Nevo’s (Nebo’s) son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife after the exile (Ezr 10:43).
ZEBOIIM

One of the “cities of the plain” that was destroyed with Sedom (Sodom) and Amorah (Gomorrah) (Dt 29:23; Hos 11:8). Tsevoim (Zeboiim) is first mentioned, with Sedom, Amorah, and Admah, as one of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) cities in the “table of nations” in Genesis 10:19. It later appears confederated with the same states (including Tsoar (Zoar)) in the battle against Amrafel (Amraphel) king of Shin’ar (Shinar), Areyok (Arioch) king of Elasar (Ellasar), Kedorlaomer king of Eylam (Elam), and Tidal king of Goiim (Gn 14:2, 8).
See also Cities of the Plain.
ZEBOIM
1. KJV spelling of Tsevoim (Zeboiim) in Genesis 10:19, Deuteronomy 29:23, and Hosea 11:8. See Zeboiim.
2. Valley where one of the raiding parties of the Pelishtim (Philistines) turned toward the border of the wilderness (1 Sm 13:18). It may be identified with Shuk ed-Dubba.
3. One of the villages outside of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) where the Benjaminites settled after the exile (Neh 11:34).
ZEBUDAH*

ZEBULUN, Tribe of

His tribe was divided into three clans named after his three sons: the Sardim (Seredites), the Elonites, and the Yahle’elim (Jahleelites) (Gn 46:14; Nm 26:27). At the census taken on the plains of Moav (Moab), the number of men in the tribe over 20 years of age and fit for military service was 60,500 (Nm 26:26-27).

The territory allotted to Zevulun’s tribe was in central Kena’an (Canaan) and included the valley of Yizre’el (Jezreel), but the boundary lines given in Joshua 19:10-16 are difficult to trace because only the tribe’s southeastern and eastern borders are indicated. The western border on the Mediterranean side is not clearly defined. In the blessing of Mosheh (Moses) (Dt 33:18-19), Zevulun, along with Yisakar (Issachar), “shall draw out [lit. suck] the abundance of the sea,” which would seem to indicate that Zevulun would have access to the sea (Mediterranean) and therefore to the mercantile and maritime trade.

The boundary details, however, do not bring Zevulun in touch geographically with the sea, in apparent contradiction to Genesis 49:13. But this reference may not imply actual contact with the Mediterranean. Zevulun’s position did enable it to profit by maritime trade because the great caravan route to the sea passed through Zevuluni (Zebulunite) territory. In addition, Zevulun’s “lot,” with its fruitful fields and valleys, ensured olive groves, vineyards, and splendid harvests. In 1 Chronicles 12:40 the tribe was able to provide rich provisions for David. Throughout the centuries the tribe maintained its identity.

Clearly, then, the tribe of Zevulun held a strong position among its tribal neighbors around Galil (Galilee) and was settled more securely. In contrast to the tribes of Asher and Naftali (Naphtali), who continued to live among the Kena’anim (Canaanites) (Jgs 1:32-33), the Kena’anim constituted a minority in Zevulun. Throughout the period of the judges the tribe was very active. For example, the victorious army in the battle of Kishon was composed of men of Zevulun and Naftali (4:6-10); in the Song of Deborah, Zevulun is praised as a people that puts its life in jeopardy to the point of death (5:18). According to Judges 6:35, the men of Zevulun took part in Gid’on’s (Gideon’s) struggle with the Midyanites (Midianites) on the plain of Yizre’el and fought with outstanding valor. The judge Eylon (Elon) belonged to the tribe of Zevulun (12:11-12), and since Galil was in the territory of Zevulun (Jos 19:15), Ivtsan (Ibzan) of Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) was probably also a Zevuluni. Another indication of the strength and importance of Zevulun’s tribe within the united kingdom period is found in the mention of Zevulun’s fighting force as the largest of the western tribal armies that fought under King David (1 Chr 12:33).

In the NT there are two references to Zevulun. The first notes Zevulun as a region into which Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), the great light, made an appearance (Mt 4:13-15). The second mention of Zevulun appears in the list of the 12 tribes in Revelation 7:8 after Yisakar.

ZECHARIAH, Book of

Longest book of the Minor Prophets and the most difficult to understand. One reason for this difficulty is the numerous visions that call for an interpreter. At times an interpreting angel is present to tell what the vision means (Zec 1:9-10, 19-20; 4:1-6; 5:5-6), but at other times, when an interpretation is really needed, there is no angel to give one. The obscure meaning of many passages has spawned numerous theories concerning the date, authorship, unity, and interpretation of this book. One thing that makes the book of Zekaryah (Zechariah) significant for the Christian is its use in the NT. The last part of Zekaryah (chs 9–11) is the most quoted section of the Prophets in the Gospel Passion narratives, and, other than Yehezkel (Ezekiel), Zekaryah influenced the book of Revelation more than any other OT book.

Author

The name Zekaryah probably means “the Lord remembers” or “the Lord is renowned.” Zekaryah is a common name in the OT and NT. At least 30 different people in the OT are named Zekaryah. There is a problem in identifying the prophet’s father. In Zechariah 1:1 and 1:7, the prophet is called “the son of Berekyah (Berechiah), the son of Iddo,” but in Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 he is called simply “the son of Iddo.” There was another Zekaryah in Yeshayah’s (Isaiah’s) time whose father was named Yeverekyah (Jeberechiah) (Is 8:2). Another prophet by the name of Zekaryah, the son of Yehoyada (Jehoiada) the priest, lived much earlier during the reign of Yoash (Joash), king of Yehudah (Judah) (835–796 BC). This prophet was stoned to death because he proclaimed that the Lord had forsaken his people because of their sins (2 Chr 24:20-22). Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) seemed to refer to this or a similar unrecorded incident, but he calls the prophet the son of Berekyah, the last of the martyrs among the prophets (Mt 23:35). However, Lukas’s (Luke’s) account of what Yeshua said about Zekaryah (Lk 11:51) does not include the words “the son of Berekyah.” Since Yeshua was quoting 2 Chronicles, which was the last book in the Hebrew Bible, he was simply indicating the sweep of time from the first murder (Hevel (Abel)) to the last (Zekaryah, the son of Yehoyada). There is no evidence that the prophet of the book of Zekaryah was martyred; therefore, the best solution to the problem is to consider Berekyah the father, and Iddo the grandfather, of this prophet.
Date

The first part of the book of Zekaryah (chs 1–8) is easy to date. The first date is in the first verse, “the eighth month of the second year of Dareyavesh (Darius).” This was Dareyavesh, king of Paras (Persia) (521–486 BC). The eighth month of Dareyavesh’s second year would be October 520 BC. This date seems to be the first time the “word of the Lord” came to Zekaryah. The second date in Zekaryah is in 1:7: “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month which is the month of Shevat (Shebat), in the second year of Dareyavesh . . .” (rsv). This date would be February 15, 519 BC. The word of the Lord that came to Zekaryah on this date seems to include the account of eight night visions, along with some oracles, from an angel who talked with him. The third date in Zekaryah is in 7:1: “In the fourth year of King Dareyavesh . . . on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Kislev (Chislev) . . .” (rsv). This date would be the equivalent of December 7, 518 BC.

There are no dates in Zechariah 9–14. Zekaryah’s (Zechariah’s) name is never mentioned, and neither is Dareyavesh or any king. A period of relative peace and stability gives place to war. The temple is standing (11:13; 14:20), and evidently Greek soldiers are present (9:13). Any attempt to assign specific dates to Zechariah 9–14 would be speculation.
Background

The temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was destroyed by Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Bavel (Babylon), in 586 BC. Nevukadnetsar made several raids against Yerushalem before and after it fell, taking many captives to Bavel (cf. 2 Kgs 24:1-17; Dn 1:1). On two occasions, Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) had predicted that captivity would last 70 years (Jer 25:11; 29:10; cf. Dn 9:2). In the time of Zekaryah, the period of 70 years since the fall of Yerushalem was coming to an end (Zec 1:12; 7:5). It had been 66 years since Yerushalem fell, when the first “word of the Lord” came to Zekaryah in the second year of Dareyavesh (520 BC). The Babylonian Empire had fallen to the Persians in 538 BC, and Koresh (Cyrus) the first king of Paras signed a decree permitting all captives to return to their homes (2 Chr 36:23; Ezr 1:1-4). Evidently, the first contingent of Jewish captives returned to Yerushalem with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) and Yehoshua (Joshua) the priest about 536 BC. One of the first objectives of the returnees was to rebuild the temple (Ezr 1:3), but internal strife and external opposition from the Shomronim (Samaritans) prohibited the immediate rebuilding of the temple. After Dareyavesh I became king of Paras in 521 BC, a wave of expectation and enthusiasm swept over the Jewish communities in Yerushalem and Bavel. Two prophets, possibly from the Babylonian exiles, Hagay (Haggai) and Zekaryah, began preaching so powerfully that work on the second temple began in 520 BC and was finished in 516 BC (Ezr 5:1, 14-15; Hg 1–2; Zec 1–8).

The book of Zekaryah opens in the second year of Dareyavesh (520 BC). Some of the captives had been back in Yerushalem for 16 years, but nothing was being done about rebuilding the temple. Zekaryah’s first message called for the people to repent and not repeat the mistake of their fathers, whose sins and refusal to repent led to the exile and destruction of the temple (Zec 1:1-6). Then a series of eight night visions follows (1:7–6:8), assuring the people that the temple would be rebuilt by Zerubavel (1:16; 4:9; 6:15). Two verses in Zekaryah speak volumes concerning the hardships and difficulties in Yerushalem before the temple was rebuilt: “This is what Yahweh Almighty says: Take heart and finish the task! You have heard what the prophets have been saying about building the Temple of Yahweh Almighty ever since the foundation was laid. Before the work on the Temple began, there were no jobs and no wages for either people or animals. No traveler was safe from the enemy, for there were enemies on all sides. I had turned everyone against each other” (8:9-10, nlt).

The first eight chapters of Zekaryah are set against the social, political, and religious situations in Yerushalem from 520 to 518 BC. But beginning with chapter 9, historical moorings are lost. Chapter 9 opens with an oracle against Aram (Syria), including Damesek (Damascus), Tsor (Tyre), and Tsidon (Sidon), and against Peleshet (Philistia). Each of these places will be conquered and cleansed and will become like a clan in Yehudah. There is the promise of a new king coming triumphantly to Yerushalem, yet humbly riding on a donkey. His reign will be peaceful and universal. The next oracle speaks of setting the captives free, but this may not refer to the Babylonian captives, because of a reference to the Greeks. Zechariah 9–12 is almost wholly concerned with the future. Some scholars call this part apocalyptic literature. The nations attack Yerushalem and are defeated (chs 12, 14). The temple is standing (11:13), but it does not seem to have a place of great prominence in the new Yerushalem and in the kingdom of God (14:6-9).
Purpose and Message

The purpose of the book is to reassure and encourage. The restored Jewish community of 520 BC needed the assurance that the temple would be rebuilt, and later groups of God’s people needed to know that ultimately the kingdom of God would come in its fullness. There are three messages in the book of Zekaryah: the need for repentance (1:1–5:11); the eight night visions (1:7–6:8) signifying that the temple would be rebuilt and God’s glory would return to Yerushalem; and the coming kingdom of God (chs 9–14).
Content

The book of Zekaryah may be divided into two main parts: chapters 1–8 and 9–14. The first part is dated between 520 BC and 518 BC. It consists of oracles and visions of Zekaryah the son of Berekyah (Berechiah). Mainly prose, its primary concern is to assure the restored Jewish community that the temple will be rebuilt. The second part (chs 9–14) is undated. There are no references to Zekaryah. The temple is standing, and much of the language is eschatological and apocalyptic. The second part itself has two parts: chapters 9–11 and 12–14. Chapters 9 and 12 begin essentially the same way: “The oracle of the word of the Lord.”

The first part of Zekaryah (chs 1–8) has four main sections: superscription and first oracle (1:1-6); eight night visions and related oracles (1:7–6:8); the symbolic crowning of Yehoshua (6:9-15); and the question about fasting and morality (7:1–8:23).
The Superscription (1:1)

This section is dated specifically “in the eighth month” of the Babylonian calendar, which was from mid-October to mid-November. The second year of Dareyavesh (Darius), king of Paras (Persia), was 520 BC. The date is important in relating the work of Zekaryah (Zechariah) to that of Hagay (cf. Hg 1:1, 15; 2:1, 10, 18-20) and to the reconstruction of the temple under Zerubavel. The first oracle concerns the need for repentance. The first message of Zekaryah came between Hagay’s second and third message. He, like Hagay, probably attributed the failure of the crops and other hardships to a failure to rebuild the temple (cf. Hg 1:6-11). Zekaryah calls for the people to repent so that they can persevere with work on the temple.
The Eight Night Visions and Related Oracles (1:7–6:8)

These visions that Zekaryah saw in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) all seem to have been given on the night of the 24th day of the 11th month (Shevat (Shebat)) in the second year of Dareyavesh (mid-January to mid-February 519 BC). Seven of the eight visions have essentially the same form. Four of the visions begin with the words “Then I looked up and saw” (1:18; 2:1; 5:1; 6:1). One begins, “In a vision during the night” (1:8). Another begins, “Then the angel who had been talking with me returned and woke me, as though I had been asleep. ‘What do you see now?’ he asked” (4:1-2, nlt). Still another (the seventh) vision begins, “Then the angel who was talking with me came forward and said . . .” (5:5). However, the fourth vision is different from the other seven. It begins, “Then he showed me” (3:1, cf. Am 7:1, 4, 7). This message in the third person contains no interpreting angel nor any direct message to Zekaryah, as if he were merely an observer. This fourth vision is so different from the other seven that it was not a part of the original series of eight.

An overall pattern to the eight visions is not evident. Some scholars have seen some significance in the fact that the visions move from the evening or night in the first vision to the sunrise in the last vision. Others have detected some relationships in pairs of visions. The first and last visions involve horses and riders or chariots. The second and third visions involve the restoration of Yehudah (Judah) and Yerushalem (1:18-21; 2:1-5). The fourth and fifth deal with the place of the two leaders in the restored community: Yehoshua (Joshua) will be cleansed and restored as the high priest (3:1-5) and Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) the governor will complete the temple (4:1-14). The sixth and seventh visions involve the cleansing of the land. A flying scroll enters the house of every thief and false witness and consumes it (5:1-4). Wickedness personified as a woman will be carried in an ephah (basket) to the land of Shin’ar (Shinar) (vv 5-11). Interspersed in the vision accounts are four oracles (1:14-17; 2:8-13; 3:6-10; 4:8-14). Each of these passages begins with the messenger formula, “Thus says the Lord,” or the expression “Cry out” (1:14, 17). The first oracle assures the people that the temple, the cities, and the choice of Yerushalem will be renewed. The second oracle exhorts any exiles remaining in Bavel (Babylon) to return to Yehudah and Yerushalem (2:7-12). Zechariah 2:12-13 are interesting. Verse 12 is the only OT reference to Palestine as “the Holy Land,” and verse 13 is similar to the call to worship in Habakkuk 2:20: “Be silent before Yahweh, all humanity, for he is springing into action from his holy dwelling” (Zec 2:13, nlt). The third oracle in the visionary accounts concerns Yehoshua the high priest as a sign of the coming of God’s servant, the Branch who removes the guilt of the land in a single day (3:6-10).
The Symbolic Crowning of Yehoshua (6:9-15)

Zekaryah is told to go into the house of Yoshiyah (Josiah) son of Tsefanyah (Zephaniah), take silver and gold from some returnees from Bavel, make a crown, and put it on the head of Yehoshua the priest as a symbol of the royal and priestly king, the Branch, the builder of the temple. After the ceremony the crown is to be hung in the temple as a memorial of those who gave the silver and the gold. The last verse (6:15) seems to say that just as gold and silver from exiles was used to symbolize the crowning of the coming king of the kingdom, so exiles, “those who are far off,” will also participate in the completion of the temple. Then Zekaryah’s hearers will know God sent him to prophesy. This will all take place when and if they will diligently obey the voice of the Lord.
The Question about Fasting and Morality (7:1–8:23)

A delegation from Beyt-El (Bethel) (10 miles or 16.1 kilometers north of Yerushalem) came to Yerushalem in the fourth year of Dareyavesh (518 BC). Work on the temple had been going on for two years. The purpose of this visit was to entreat the favor of the Lord (7:2) and to ask the priests and the prophets if they should continue to fast as they had done since the temple was destroyed 70 years earlier (v 3). The Lord told Zekaryah to ask why they were fasting—for the Lord or for selfish motives? The answer to the question of fasting seems to be that God desires truth, justice, and covenant-love more than fasting. Zekaryah reiterates the message the Lord had already given his people by the former prophets. The last section in the first part of Zekaryah is a decalogue of promises (8:1-23). The ten promises begin with the words “Thus says the Lord” or “The word of the Lord came to me.” The last word of God is not judgment but promise, hope, forgiveness, and restoration.
The Oracles of the Lord (chs 9–12)

The last half of the book of Zekaryah (chs 9–14) falls into two nearly equal parts: chapters 9–11 (46 verses) and chapters 12–14 (44 verses). Each part begins with the words “An oracle” (9:1; 12:1). Both “oracles” are primarily eschatological. The first part (chs 9–11) is concerned with the restoration of the tribes to Palestine (9:11-17; 10:6-12). In order to accomplish this, the Lord will rid Palestine and Aram (Syria) of opponents to his rule (9:1-8; 11:1-3), remove the evil shepherds (rulers; 10:2b-5; 11:4-17), and the Prince of Peace will come (9:9-10). The last “oracle” of Zekaryah (12:1–14:21) is also eschatological. This time the concern is primarily that of Yerushalem and Yehudah. Twice Yerushalem is attacked by the nations (12:1-8; 14:1-5). Each time the Lord fights for Yerushalem, Yehudah, and the house of David. Yerushalem weeps and mourns for an unidentified martyr (12:10-14). The martyr could be called the “good” shepherd who is killed and his sheep scattered (13:7-9). Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) referred to this passage in connection with his arrest (Mt 26:31; Mk 14:27). A fountain will be opened for the house of David, and the inhabitants of Yerushalem will be cleansed from sin, idolatry, and false prophets (Zec 13:1-6). The new Yerushalem will remain aloft on its site and the land around it will be turned into a plain (14:10-11). There will be no night nor extreme temperatures in the new Yerushalem. Living waters will flow from Yerushalem, and the Lord will become King of all the earth. Those who fight against Yerushalem will be destroyed, but those who survive will worship the Lord year by year by keeping the Feast of Booths.

The last scene in the book of Zekaryah is a picture of the world after Harmagedon (Armageddon), a new world cleansed of sin. It will be a time of peace and security. When God comes to reign, everything will become holy. The warhorses will become as holy as the priest’s turban, and the ordinary cooking vessel will be as temple vessels. The Kena’ani (Canaanite) or trader will be eliminated. There will be no difference between Yehudi (Jew) and Gentile, as long as one worships the Lord of Hosts as King.

ZEDEKIAH

1. Yehudah’s (Judah’s) last king and a key political figure in the fateful final decade of the southern kingdom. His reign (597–586 BC) spanned Nevukadnetsar’s (Nebuchadnezzar’s) two attacks on Yerushalem (Jerusalem), in 597 and 586. The first attack was in reprisal for the rebellion of Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) son, Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) (609–598 BC), against Nevukadnetsar; however, by the time his forces captured Yerushalem, Yehoyakim was dead and had been succeeded by his 18-year-old son Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin). Nevukadnetsar deposed the young king and deported him to Bavel (Babylon), along with the elite of the nation: government officials, army officers, and craftsmen. As Yehoyakin’s replacement, Nevukadnetsar appointed his uncle Matanyah (Mattaniah), a younger brother of Yehoyakim and of the earlier, short-lived King Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz) (609 BC). Matanyah was thus the third son of Yoshiyah to occupy the throne of Yehudah. The Babylonian king named him Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah), which means “the Lord is my righteousness.”

Tsidkiyah found himself in a difficult position as Yehudah’s king. Many evidently still regarded Yehoyakin as the real king (cf. Jer 28:1-4). Certainly the Yehudim (Judeans) deported to Bavel dated events by reference to Yehoyakin (2 Kgs 25:27; Ez 1:2). Though the Babylonians exacted from Tsidkiyah an oath of loyalty (2 Chr 36:13; Ez 17:13-18), evidence suggests that they too viewed Tsidkiyah’s predecessor as the legitimate king and Tsidkiyah as regent. They may have been holding him in reserve for possible restoration to power, should events require it.

Yehudah was filled with a false optimism that could hardly have helped the new king. It was confidently expected that the deportation of the leading citizens would be only temporary; prophets were guaranteeing that Bavel’s power would be broken within two years (Jer 28:2-4). They were opposed by a few prophets led by Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), whose message found little support.

Pressure both from within the nation and from without was put on Tsidkiyah to change his political allegiance. In the fourth year of his reign (593 BC), the neighboring states of Amon (Ammon), Moav (Moab), Tsor (Tyre), and Tsidon (Sidon) formed a coalition to fight for independence from Bavel. Envoys were sent to Tsidkiyah (Jer 27:1-3). However, Yirmiyah advised the king not to get involved. In the same year, according to Jeremiah 51:59, Tsidkiyah visited Bavel. He may have been summoned to affirm his loyalty and to explain his role in the political situation. The planned rebellion did not occur, perhaps because aid from Mitsrayim (Egypt) failed to materialize.

Within the Yehudi (Judean) court a strong pro-Egyptian party existed. This party saw Mitsrayim as an ally for breaking away from their eastern master, just like the advisers of King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) a century before (cf. Is 31:1-3; 36:6). Tsidkiyah, finding it difficult to resist this political pressure, eventually transferred his allegiance to Mitsrayim.

Hofra (Hophra) (589–570 BC), Psammetichus’s heir to the Mitsri (Egyptian) throne, organized a joint rebellion in the west against Bavel. According to Ezekiel 21:18-32 and 25:12-17, Yehudah and Amon supported him, while Edom and Peleshet (Philistia) shrewdly abstained. Tsidkiyah was rebuked by the prophet Yehezkel (Ezekiel) (Ez 17:13-18) for breaking his oath to Nevukadnetsar (cf. 2 Chr 36:13) and rebelling against him by sending envoys to Mitsrayim to negotiate for military support.

In the face of this western uprising engineered by his Mitsri rival, Nevukadnetsar was forced to march westward. Setting up headquarters at Rivlah (Riblah) in northern Aram (Syria), he decided to make Yerushalem his prime target (Ez 21:18-23). The ensuing siege of Yerushalem was temporarily lifted due to an Mitsri attack but afterward was resumed until the city fell. Tsidkiyah, fleeing eastward with his troops, was caught near Yeriho (Jericho) and taken north to Nevukadnetsar at Rivlah. There he was put on trial for breaking his promises of vassalage. By way of punishment, his sons were killed before his eyes. This tragic sight was the last he ever saw, since his eyes were then put out. He was taken in chains to Bavel, where he eventually died in prison (2 Kgs 25:5-7; Jer 39:7; 52:8-11; cf. Ez 12:13).

Author

According to the editorial heading (Zep 1:1), Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) prophesied during the reign of Yoshiyah (Josiah) (640–609 BC). His family tree is given in an unusually full form. Some scholars have suggested that his great-great-grandfather was King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (715–686 BC). But remarkably there is no Jewish or Christian tradition to support the suggestion, which there probably would have been if it had been true. His own name, meaning “he whom the Lord protects or hides,” was not uncommon and was a testimony to the keeping power of God.
Date, Origin, and Destination

Tsefanyah probably prophesied around 630 BC. The fall of Nineveh (612 BC) had not yet occurred (2:13-15). Yoshiyah’s reign falls into two periods, dividing at 622 BC. In that year, while the temple was being cleared of pagan articles, the Book of the Law was found, which gave momentum to Yoshiyah’s religious reforms (2 Kgs 22). The unreformed state of affairs described by Tsefanyah (Zep 1:4-12; 3:1-4) points to a date before 622, at least for his denunciations. The prophet addressed Yehudah (Judah), the southern kingdom, and in particular the civil and religious authorities in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). He most probably prophesied during the reign of Yoshiyah, who came to the throne at the age of eight.

The negative parts of the book concerning the sin and punishment of Yehudah—now fulfilled—would serve as a serious warning against disobedience to God. Moreover, the fulfillment of Tsefanyah’s prophetic threats would serve to enhance the positive side of the book, confirming the hope of completion in the experience of a fresh generation of God’s people.
Background

Politically, the Assyrian Empire had spread westward and held Palestine in its grip. The long reign of Menasheh (Manasseh) (696–642 BC) had been a period of total subservience to Ashur (Assyria). Political subservience as an Assyrian vassal meant religious subservience to the gods of Ashur, especially worship of the heavenly bodies (2 Kgs 21:5). Tsefanyah complained of this sin (Zep 1:5). When the door opened to one foreign religion, others naturally came in. Once the exclusiveness of the worship of the God of Yisrael (Israel) was abandoned, Palestinian cults were openly accepted. The Kena’ani (Canaanite) Ba’al (Baal) was blatantly worshiped (2 Kgs 21:3), as Tsefanyah attested (Zep 1:4). Tsefanyah condemned the worshipers of Molek (Molech) (v 5), who sacrificed children to the Amoni (Ammonite) god (1 Kgs 11:7; 2 Kgs 23:10). International imperialism meant a weakening of national culture, so that foreign customs were practiced, probably with religious overtones (Zep 1:8-9).

The reign of Yoshiyah brought changes, marking a political and religious turning point. Ashur, preoccupied with troubles on the eastern and northern frontiers and unable to consolidate its acquisitions, became unable to reinforce its authority in the west. This weakness induced Yoshiyah to launch a national liberation movement. He threw off the yoke of Ashur and expanded his sphere of influence northward into the territory of the old northern kingdom. From a religious standpoint, he completely dissociated himself and his country from the religions that prevailed in Yehudah and recalled the nation to a pure and exclusive faith in the God of Yisrael. The book of Tsefanyah shows that there was at least one person who shared his ideals. His prophetic ministry undoubtedly paved the way for Yoshiyah’s subsequent reformation. He was a contemporary of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), at least for the early part of that prophet’s career (Yirmiyah began prophesying in 627 BC).

Scholars have suggested that Tsefanyah’s prophesying was prompted in part by attacks of the Scythians. The Greek historian Herodotus tells how the barbaric Scythians overran western Asia and reached as far south as the Mitsri (Egyptian) frontier at about the time that Tsefanyah prophesied. There is now much less inclination to believe Herodotus’s tale and relate Tsefanyah’s prophetic ministry to it. There is no objective evidence for Skuthais (Scythian) attacks on so large a scale as Herodotus claimed. Probably Tsefanyah spoke simply out of a theological necessity, as he himself claimed (e.g., 1:17). From his inspired standpoint, he foresaw that a clash involving divine intervention and human downfall was unavoidable.
Purpose and Teaching

As Tsefanyah prophesied in God’s name, he denounced the religious sins of Yehudah and the corruption rampant among both civil and religious authorities. He foretold the downfall of the nation that actually occurred in 586 BC. The moral and religious landslide could only culminate in a political avalanche of destruction that would engulf the nation. This avalanche is called by Tsefanyah “the Day of the Lord.” It was not a new term, and the prophet knew that it would arouse terror in the hearts of his hearers. Amos used it, and even in his time it was well established (Am 5:18-20). Yeshayah (Isaiah) was the first to use the expression in the southern kingdom (Is 2:6-22, see v 12). In this, as in a number of respects, Tsefanyah was a latter-day Yeshayah called by God to reapply truths earlier prophesied by Yeshayah to a later generation.

The theme of the Day of the Lord refers to a time when the Lord would decisively intervene in the world to establish his sovereignty. Hostile elements would be swept aside. The enemies of God, sinners against his moral will, would be exposed and punished. It was associated with judgment upon those who did not acknowledge God’s sovereignty—especially Gentiles, but also sinful Yisrael. The emphasis on the suffering of God’s people was intended to correct the popular assumption that other nations would be the sole target of divine judgment.

The “day” also would vindicate those who were loyal to God. It guaranteed the rehabilitation of his oppressed supporters. Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) developed this two-sided phenomenon in order to communicate the truth of God to his own generation. It is “a day of the wrath of God” (Zep 1:15, 18; 2:2), when his reaction to human sin would be demonstrated. Its target was not only other nations but Yehudah as well, both Yerushalem, the capital (1:10-13), and the other cities of Yehudah.

Tsefanyah also had a positive message for the people of Yehudah. For the prophets, the message of salvation did not cancel the message of doom. Judgment would come first, then salvation would follow. But the period of tribulation could not be avoided. The prophet’s grim descriptions of “the day of wrath” are interpreted as dire warnings and implicit pleas to the people of Yehudah to abandon their complacent, sinful ways.

Clearly, Tsefanyah’s role under God was to reapply earlier truths sadly forgotten by his own generation. Tsefanyah was able to foresee God’s judgment of Yehudah (Judah) and the world. But he also proclaimed permanent truths concerning the nature of God and his providential relationship to the world and concerning the responsibilities of the people of God.

The importance of the book of Tsefanyah for the NT lies in the phraseology about the Day of the Lord. There are a number of allusions to this aspect of his message (Mt 13:41 [Zep 1:3]; Rv 6:17 [1:14]; 14:5 [3:13]; 16:1 [3:8]). These echoes stress Tsefanyah’s importance beyond his own time. He contributed to the total biblical picture of a God who intervenes in human history and will establish his kingdom. Tsefanyah’s descriptions are a pattern for events that will mark the end of history.
Content
The heading (Zep 1:1) introduces Tsefanyah, gives the historical setting, and above all stresses his meditation on the divine word.

The first major part of the book is 1:2–2:3. It subdivides into four units: verses 2-7, 8-13, 14-18; 2:1-3. Verses 2-7 include Yehudah in a forecast of universal destruction. Tsefanyah used traditional material to stress that God’s people were by no means exempt, as they often chose to believe (cf. Am 5:18-20). The prophet supported his startling revelation with reasoned statements regarding the religious deviations practiced in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). The image of sacrifice was used ironically, portraying Yehudah as the victim.

The national administration and members of the royal family were guilty (Zep 1:8-13). Superstitions were punctiliously observed, yet basic divine commands against stealing and fraudulent gain went unheeded. Tsefanyah saw the enemy attack on the north side of Yerushalem as an illustration of God’s punishment of dishonest traders (cf. Am 8:5-6; Mi 6:10-11).

There follows a shocking and terrifying description of the grimness of the coming “Day” (Zep 1:14-18). The prophet stirred up a complacent people who did not want to hear God’s message. He frightened them into reality with a monotonous drumbeat of doom and destruction. Yehudah would be the demoralized target of God’s wrath. Their wealth had secured luxurious imports but could not prevent divine judgment.

The prophet completed his sermon with an appeal for repentance (2:1-3). Having emotionally stirred his audience from their apathy, he was able to bring the good news that all was not yet lost. A penitential assembly at the temple and the intercession of the spiritually minded and obedient among God’s people might prevent destruction. God’s punishment of foreign nations is described in the second main part of the book (2:4-15). Representative states are named to the west, east, south, and north of Yehudah. In the context of the previous material, it amplifies the universal nature of the Day of the Lord. Like the first part, it subdivides into four passages: verses 2:4-7, 8-11, 12, and 13-15.

The subject of the first passage is the Pelishtim (Philistines). In the case of the cities of Azah (Gaza) and Ekron, there is a play on words typical of Hebrew prophecy. Both names contain doom within their very sound. The Pelishtim are labeled as trespassers because they were illegal immigrants from Kraitai (Crete) into the Promised Land, which was intended for God’s own people.

Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) predicted that Moav (Moab) and Amon (Ammon) would suffer attack for their overbearing attitude and their annexation of Yehudi (Judean) territory (2:8-11). God would come to the aid of his covenant people.

The first two main sections have spelled out at length a message of judgment for both Yehudah and the surrounding nations. This twofold message is now repeated in a much shorter form in the third main section (3:1-8). Tsefanyah criticized Yerushalem in its combined role of political capital and religious center. The responsibility of being God’s representatives rested too lightly on the shoulders of government and temple officials. Civil leaders abused their powers by demanding bribes and even killing their political opponents. Instead of being the shepherds of the people (cf. Ez 34), they were beasts of prey (cf. Ez 22:25-27). The prophets misused their gifts for their own selfish interests, while the priests broke the strict regulations of the temple. The lessons of history went unheeded; they had not learned caution and reverence. The conclusion is clear: Yehudah could not escape punishment in the coming Day of the Lord but would suffer with other nations.

The outworking of God’s will for both Yehudah (Judah) and the nations is in view in the final main section (Zep 3:9-20), but this time from a quite different aspect. Punishment was not God’s last word for his own people or even for the nations at large. Ultimately God’s will is not destruction but salvation (2 Pt 3:9). The section has three parts: Zephaniah 3:9-10, 11-13, and 14-20. Verses 9-10 deal with the conversion of the nations. This remarkable passage looks forward with divinely guaranteed certainty to the willing submission of Gentiles to the God of Yisrael (Israel). Their turning to God would not be based on human initiative but would originate in the providential activity of God. Lips defiled by worship of pagan gods would be purified and devoted solely to the adoration of the God of Yisrael. People from remote parts of the earth, here illustrated as the remote south beyond the Kushi (Ethiopian) Nile, would come as suppliants, as if they were scattered Yehudim (Jews) returning home.

God’s own people would be marked by a change of heart (3:11-13). By now they would have been purged of the proud people who put themselves before God in the sphere of politics and religion. They would be a purified people who humbly trusted in God. To them were promised the blessings of paradise.

The last passage speaks of coming joys (3:14-20). The prophet projects himself into the future, to the time when God’s judgment would be over and the time of salvation had dawned. God’s people would rejoice in the presence of their Lord. Fear and demoralization would be canceled by God’s powerful presence and radiant joy. His joy would infectiously communicate itself to them so that they too would rejoice. Moreover, his joy would be a reaction to the transformation he was working in the lives of his people (v 17; “he will renew you in his love,” rsv). A necessary part of this transformation would feature the vindication of God’s suffering people. They would be brought to a position of honor, as the visible representatives of the God of glory. Ultimately, God’s power would be revealed through a people of power.

ZERUBBABEL

Babylonian-born Yehudi (Jew) who returned to Palestine in 538 BC to serve as governor of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) under Persian rule. The name presumably means “seed [offspring] of Bavel (Babylon),” referring to someone born in Bavel.

The exact identity of Zerubavel’s (Zerubbabel’s) biological father is uncertain. All biblical references except one mention Shealtiyel (Shealtiel) as his father (Ezr 3:2, 8; 5:2; Neh 12:1; Hg 1:1, 12-14; 2:2, 23; Mt 1:12-13; Lk 3:27). This would make Zerubavel the grandson of the Davidic king Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin). However, 1 Chronicles 3:19 identifies Pedayah (Pedaiah), the brother of Shealtiyel, as Zerubavel’s father.

Two solutions have been proposed. Many scholars have assumed that Shealtiyel died before fathering an heir. His brother, Pedayah, would then have fathered Zerubavel by Shealtiyel’s widow. Hence, Zerubavel would have retained the name of Shealtiyel rather than Pedayah in accordance with the law of levirate marriage (Dt 25:5-10). This solution is weakened by its lack of textual support; similarly, the Chronicler would hardly have failed to state such an important piece of information if he had been desirous of “correcting” an error pertaining to Zerubavel’s parentage.

A simpler solution is obtained by reading the Septuagint text of 1 Chronicles 3:19, which lists Salathiail (Salathiel) (Shealtiyel) as the father of Zerubavel. In this way, the single reference to 1 Chronicles may be harmonized with the other verses cited above.

In either case, whether Shealtiyel or Pedayah was Zerubavel’s biological father, it is clear that Zerubavel was of Davidic lineage and was viewed by members of the Israeli (Israelite) community as a viable candidate for leading them back to a position of power.

Following the edict of Koresh (Cyrus) in 538 BC, Yehudim (Jews) were permitted to return to Palestine and reclaim their former homeland. Zerubavel was appointed governor, and probably by the decade of 529–520 had started work on the reconstruction of the Yerushalem temple. However, because of several discouraging events, little was accomplished until the year 520 BC.

The writings of Hagay (Haggai) and Zekaryah (Zechariah) reveal much information about Zerubavel’s standing in the community. These two prophets evidently viewed Yeshua (Jeshua) and Zerubavel as the two men chosen by God for the task. Accordingly, in many of their oracles, support for one or both men is openly stated (e.g., Hg 2:21-23; Zec 3:8; 4:6-7; 6:12). The prophets viewed Yeshua and Zerubavel’s work as being messianic. This is most clearly seen in the vision of Zekaryah (Zec 4:11-14). In the vision, two olive branches, one on either side of the lampstand, are identified as “the two anointed who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.” As the context clearly shows, none other than Yeshua (or Yehoshua (Joshua); named in 3:1-9) and Zerubavel (named in 4:6-10) are meant. Because of his association with the rebuilding of the temple in Yerushalem, Zerubavel had been accorded a place of great honor in Jewish tradition.
Some hold that Zerubavel was known to the Persians as Sheshebatsar (Sheshbazzar). See Sheshbazzar.

ZEUS

Chief god of the Greek pantheon (Roman Jupiter). Zeus was initially worshiped as part of an animistic cult, as the sky god with thunder as his principal manifestation. Well before the time of Homer, however, Zeus had become the preeminent personal god of the Greek residents of Thessaly, with Mt Olympus serving as the focal point of the cult. By NT times, Zeus was considered the Greek father god who possessed supreme powers. The quotation Paulos (Paul) used in Acts 17:28 from Cleanthes (and/or Aratus) was originally ascribed to Zeus (“in him we live and move and have our being”).

Zeus is most significant in biblical writings as a result of Paulos and Barnabas’s encounter with the priest of Zeus at Lustra (Lystra) (Acts 14:8-18). Because Paulos and Barnabas had healed a lame man, the residents of Lustra attempted to worship them, identifying Barnabas with Zeus and Paulos with Hermes, the messenger of the gods. It was not unusual that this misidentification should take place, since the Greek gods were frequently represented as taking on human appearances and intervening directly in human affairs. Unlike the true God, Zeus and his consorts were often viewed as capriciously bestowing favor or disfavor. The attribution of “divinity” to Paulos and Barnabas allowed them to identify the key differences between Greek and Christian theology.

ZIBA

Former servant of Sha’ul (Saul) whom David commissioned to find survivors of the house of Sha’ul so that he might “show them kindness” (2 Sm 9:2-12). In the period following Sha’ul’s death, Tsiva (Ziba) apparently had not only gained his freedom but had also become a successful landowner. This status was lost as a result of the discovery of Mefiboshet (Mephibosheth), Yonatan’s (Jonathan’s) crippled son. Tsiva later became involved in a controversy with Mefiboshet concerning Mefiboshet’s failure to accompany David when he fled during Avshalom’s (Absalom’s) rebellion (2 Sm 16:1-4; 19:17, 24-29). Most commentators have blamed Tsiva with duplicity and slander in the affair, but the text allows no certain conclusion as to who was guilty. On Mefiboshet’s behalf, it is unlikely that he would have believed that he could inherit the throne, as Tsiva had claimed (2 Sm 16:3). Mefiboshet also seems to have been loyal to David (though it is possible that David brought him to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to ensure that he would be under protective surveillance). In Tsiva’s defense, it is notable that David did believe without question that Mefiboshet might have had aspirations for the throne. Tsiva also appears consistently as a loyal supporter of David in spite of the fact that David’s decision had cost him his independent status (2 Sm 16:1; 19:17). Of course, Tsiva’s displeasure at his loss of independence might have motivated him to defame Mefiboshet. In any case, David appears to have had reason to doubt both versions of the truth. Rather than supporting either claim, he chose to divide the land between them (2 Sm 19:29).

ZIGGURAT*

Term meaning “temple tower”; a ziggurat was similar in profile to the step pyramid of Mitsrayim (Egypt) and was used for worship. They were frequent in the major cities of Mesopotamia. The Tower of Bavel (Babel) (Gn 11:1-9) is believed to have been of this construction. It was widely believed that deities dwelt above, in high places. Therefore, worship was more appropriate on hills or mountains. There are no hills in Mesopotamia, nor is there building stone. Consequently, the inhabitants built with mud brick. The ziggurats of mud brick were constructed as substitutes for hills, where the worshiper or priest could get closer to the gods. Like the pyramids of Mitsrayim, these temple towers were square. Instead of having sloping sides, there was a succession of terraces, each smaller than the one below. Access to each level was by stairways or ramps. The shrine or altar was on top, where the priests would officiate at sacrifices, incantations, and prayers. The great seven-story ziggurat at Bavel measured nearly 300 feet (91.4 meters) on a side at the base and rose to about the same height.

ZIN, Wilderness of

Area lying in the northern portion of the Sinay (Sinai) Peninsula, while the wilderness of Sin lies in the southern portion. It is one of the four or five “wildernesses” of the Sinay Peninsula, the others being the wilderness of Paran (Gn 21:21), the wilderness of Shur (Ex 15:22), and the wilderness of Sinay (Nm 9:1) and the wilderness of Sin (Nm 33:11). The area identified as the wilderness of Tsin (Zin) is associated with the village of Tsin (Nm 34:4). The wilderness was west of Edom, southwest of the Dead Sea, and south of Yehudah (Judah). Within this arid area were four copious springs or oases, including Kadesh-Barnea (Kadesh-barnea). Most of the 38 years the Israelis (Israelites) spent in the Sinay Desert were spent in this area. From the wilderness of Tsin the spies were dispatched to spy out the land of Kena’an (Canaan) (Nm 13:1-26; 32:8). Here also the rebels were sentenced to die because of their unbelief (14:22-23). Mosheh (Moses) sinned by failing to give God the credit for bringing water out of the rock (20:1-13; 27:14), and Miryam (Miriam), his sister, died and was buried here (20:1). This area was remembered as the “great and terrible wilderness” (Dt 1:19; 8:15).

ZION

The Yevusi (Jebusite) fortress in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) conquered by David. Thereafter, Tsiyon (Zion) was used by biblical writers to identify other areas of Yerushalem and was used as a designation of the entire city. Tsiyon was also used to describe, spiritually speaking, the eternal city of God.
Geographical Sites
The Yevusi Fortress

The first occurrence of the word “Tsiyon” is in the narrative of David’s conquest of Yerushalem (2 Sm 5:6-10; 1 Chr 11:4-9). David captured the “fortress of Tsiyon,” which was thereafter known as the “city of David.” The “fortress of Tsiyon” may refer to the entire walled perimeter of the approximately 11-acre (4.5-hectare) site on the southeastern ridge (the Ofel (Ophel) Ridge), or to a smaller fortified area within that site.
The Temple Mount

Changes in the perimeter of the city by incorporating more territory within the walls extend the term Tsiyon. When Shelomoh (Solomon) built the temple and his palace and extended the walls north of the Ofel Ridge to encompass the threshing floor of Ornan the Yevusi (2 Sm 24:16-18; 1 Chr 21:15-18, 28), the name Tsiyon was applied to these areas as well. The transfer of the ark “from the city of David which is Tsiyon” (1 Kgs 8:1; 2 Chr 5:2) to the temple hill brought both an extension and a reduction of the territory embraced by the term “Tsiyon.” The whole city could still be called Tsiyon, but from this point on, there would be a close identification between Tsiyon and the temple hill. The temple precincts became the primary Tsiyon; references to Tsiyon in the poetic books and the preaching of the prophets are primarily to the temple area as the dwelling place of God.
The Entire City

The word “Tsiyon” can be used as a designation of the entire city or its population without any particular reference to the temple area. This use is clearest in poetic passages where Tsiyon is the parallel term to Yerushalem (Pss 51:18; 76:2; 102:21; 135:21; 147:12; Is 2:3; 30:19; 33:20; 37:32; 40:9; 41:27; 62:1; Jer 26:18; 51:35; Am 1:2; Zep 3:14) or to the villages of Yehudah (Judah) (Pss 69:35; 97:8; Is 40:9).
Theological Motifs
In the Old Testament

Many theological motifs attach to the Tsiyon (Zion) theme as it develops in redemptive history. The dominant motif of Tsiyon as the dwelling place of God, the place where God is in the midst of his people, is conjoined to the larger theme of Imanu-El (Immanuel), “God in our midst.” Just as the pillar of fire and cloud stood above the tabernacle during the wilderness wandering, so once Yisrael (Israel) had attained the place of God’s choosing (Dt 12:5-14), he would dwell there. When Yerushalem (Jerusalem) became David’s capital and Shelomoh had completed the temple, the glory cloud filled the temple (1 Kgs 8:10; 2 Chr 5:13-14) and Yerushalem became the dwelling place of God (Pss 74:2; 76:2; 135:21; Is 8:18; Jl 3:17-21). The Lord loved and chose Tsiyon (Pss 78:68; 132:13). His glorious presence was there, and from there he would speak (50:1-2). His fire was in Tsiyon, his furnace in Yerushalem (Is 31:8-9). There he was enthroned above the cherubim (Pss 9:11; 99:1-2) and ruled over his people and the nations (Is 24:23). His chosen king ruled from that holy hill (Pss 2:6; 48:1).

Though the size of the site of ancient Yerushalem is not particularly impressive and ordinarily would not be considered a large hill, for the psalmist Tsiyon is God’s holy hill (Ps 99:9). The prophets describe it as “chief among the mountains, raised above the hills” (Is 2:2; Mi 4:1). The Kena’ani (Canaanite) god Ba’al (Baal) was thought to dwell on a great mountain to the north, Mt Tsafon (Zaphon), so the psalmist describes Tsiyon as “beautiful in its loftiness, like the utmost heights of Mt Tsafon” (Ps 48:1-2). God’s sanctuary is “like the high mountains” (Ps 78:68; Ez 40:2).

An adequate water supply has been a problem for Yerushalem throughout its history. During the OT period, the city’s water came from one small spring. But in the eyes of the poets and prophets, Tsiyon is gladdened by a great river that brings life wherever it flows (Ps 46:4; Ez 47:1-12; Jl 3:18; Zec 13:1; 14:8; see Rv 22:1-2). The threatening waters of chaos cannot shake the city of God (Ps 46:1-3).

Because Tsiyon is the city of God, it is the object of pilgrims, Yehudi (Jew) and Gentile alike, who thirst to be in the presence of God in Tsiyon’s temple (Pss 42:1-2; 63:1). The pilgrim psalms give vivid expression to their longing (84; 122; 125–128). All humanity will come to God in Tsiyon (65:1-4). The Gentiles will make annual pilgrimages bringing gifts (Ps 76; Is 18:7; Zep 3:9-10); even former enemies will be regarded as native-born citizens of Tsiyon (Ps 87; Is 60:14; Zec 14:21). The nations will stream into Yerushalem to inaugurate an era of peace (Is 2:1-5; Mi 4:1-8). Year after year the festivals of Yisrael will be celebrated in Tsiyon by Gentiles (Zec 14:16-19).
In the New Testament

The NT further develops the emphasis on both the heavenly and the eschatological Tsiyon. For example, the author of Hebrews said that the OT saints looked “forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God . . . longing for a better country—a heavenly one” (Heb 11:10, 16, niv), but none of them received the promises because God had planned something even better (vv 39-40). The church now enjoys what believers of the old covenant could never know: unlimited access to the presence of God in that Holy City, “Mount Tsiyon, the heavenly Yerushalem, the city of the living God” (12:22; see vv 18-24). Earthly Tsiyon is but a shadow of the heavenly reality. The present city of Yerushalem is likened to a slave woman, but the heavenly Yerushalem is free and the mother of both Yehudi and Gentile (Gal 4:21-27; see Is 49:14-23; 54:1). The NT also looks forward to the eschatological expectation of the re-creation of heaven and earth and the revelation of the new Yerushalem (Rv 21:2). It is a city on a great high mountain (Rv 21:10; see Pss 48:1-2; 78:68; Is 2:2; Ez 40:2; Mi 4:1), and a river of life flows within (Rv 22:1-2).
See also Jerusalem; Jerusalem, New.
ZION, Daughter of

Term used primarily in prophetic literature to designate the inhabitants of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Tsiyon (Zion)) and its surrounding regions. The term was further applied to those in Bavel (Babylon) who had been exiled from Yerushalem and the Yehudi (Judean) countryside (Is 1:8; Jer 4:31; 6:2, 23). Since ancient cities were considered metaphorically to be the mother of their inhabitants, referring to the people of Yerushalem as “daughters of Tsiyon” was entirely appropriate, particularly in poetic literature. While Yisrael (Israel) was to be the “virgin daughter” of spiritual Tsiyon (2 Kgs 19:21; Is 37:22; Lam 2:13), many of the prophetic contexts proclaim judgment on the unfaithful “daughters” (Is 3:16-17; 4:4; Mi 1:13). Although the “daughters of Tsiyon” were judged for their unfaithfulness, the ultimate promise was that God would deliver them (Is 52:2; 62:11; Zec 9:9; Mt 21:5; Jn 12:15).
See also Zion.
ZIOR

One of the cities of the hill country allotted to Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe for an inheritance (Jos 15:54). Since it is associated with Hevron (Hebron) in the text, Tsi’or (Zior) is likely identified with modern Sa’ir, the traditional location for Esav’s (Esau’s) tomb.
ZIPH (Person)
1. Descendant of Kalev (Caleb) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:42).
2. One of the sons of Yehalel’el (Jehallelel) from Yehudah’s tribe (1 Chr 4:16).
ZIPH (Place)
1. One of the cities in the extreme south assigned to Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe for an inheritance (Jos 15:24).

2. One of the cities in the hill country belonging to Yehudah’s tribe (Jos 15:55), mentioned with Maeon (Maon), Karmel (Carmel), Yizre’el (Jezreel), and most prominently with Hevron (Hebron) (cf. 1 Chr 2:42). Zif (Ziph) has been identified with a site three miles (4.8 kilometers) south of Hevron. The surrounding wilderness region is probably the “wilderness of Zif” where David hid from Sha’ul (Saul) (1 Sm 23:14-15; 26:2). The Zifim (Ziphites) who betrayed David to Sha’ul were residents of this city and the surrounding region (1 Sm 23:19; 26:1; Ps 54 title). Zif is later mentioned as one of the cities fortified by Rehav’am (Rehoboam) (2 Chr 11:8).
ZIPHAH
Yehalel’el’s (Jehallelel’s) second son (or possibly daughter, since the form is feminine), listed in 1 Chronicles 4:16.
ZIPHIMS*
KJV rendering of Zifim (Ziphites), the inhabitants of Zif (Ziph), in the title of Psalm 54. See Ziph (Place) #2.
ZIPHITE
Inhabitant of Zif (Ziph) (1 Sm 23:19; 26:1; Ps 54 title). See Ziph (Place) #2.
ZIPHRON
Geographical landmark defining the northern boundary of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) land to be possessed by Yisrael (Israel) (Nm 34:9).
ZIPPOR
Father of the Moavi (Moabite) king Balak. Balak called on Bil’am (Balaam) to curse Yisrael (Israel) (Nm 22:2, 10, 16; 23:18; Jos 24:9; Jgs 11:25).
ZIPPORAH

Wife of Mosheh (Moses) and mother of his sons Gereshom (Gershom) and Eliezer (Ex 2:21). Though she is listed as the daughter of Re’uel (Reuel) (v 18), Re’uel was probably the father of Hovav (Hobab) (Nm 10:29; also called Yitro (Jethro), Ex 3:1; 4:18), who in turn was the father of Tsiporah (Zipporah). Tsiporah circumcised Gereshom to prevent Mosheh’s death prior to his return to Mitsrayim (Egypt) (Ex 4:25). Apparently at that point Tsiporah and the children left Mosheh and went back to live with her father, returning later during the wilderness wanderings (18:2).
ZITHER
