ZITHRI*
KJV spelling of Sitri (Sithri), Uziel’s (Uzziel’s) son, in Exodus 6:22. See Sithri.
ZIV*
Name of the Hebrew month corresponding to about mid-April to mid-May (1 Kgs 6:1, 37). See Calendars, Ancient and Modern.
ZIZ, Ascent of

Mountain pass going up from the Dead Sea to the Yehudi (Judean) highlands. This ascent was the route used by the Amonim (Ammonites) and the Moavim (Moabites) prior to their defeat by Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) as prophesied by Jehaziel (2 Chr 20:16). It is likely that Tsits (Ziz) should be identified with Ayin (Ain) Jidy, a pass that still provides an important route from the Dead Sea into the Yehudi interior.
ZIZA
1. Chief of Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) tribe descending from Shemayah (Shemaiah) (1 Chr 4:37).
2. Son of Rehav’am (Rehoboam) and Ma’akah (Maacah) (2 Chr 11:20).
3. Second of Shimei’s sons and a clan chief within the Gershoni (Gershonite) branch of Levi’s tribe (1 Chr 23:11); perhaps the same as Zina in 1 Chronicles 23:10.
ZOAN

One of the principal cities in the delta region of ancient Mitsrayim (Egypt). Tsoan (Zoan), which was variously known as Tsoan, Tsoan, Avaris, and possibly Ra’meses (Rameses) (the towns were either the same or contiguous), was located on the south shore of Lake Menzaleh at the northeastern edge of the Mitsri (Egyptian) Delta. Tsoan was rebuilt during or shortly before the Hyksos period (c. 1730 BC; Nm 13:22). Because of its strategic location on the Tanitic branch of the Nile and near Mitsrayim’s northeastern frontier, Tsoan was an important military and political base during the entire period of Mitsri native rule. It served as the capital city during the Hyksos period, as well as serving as the effective capital during the 21st through the 23d dynasties (c. 1090–718 BC) and as the northern capital during the 25th dynasty (c. 712–663 BC).

Tsoan was significant to the Israelis (Israelites) during each of its periods of ascendancy. Whether the exodus occurred early (c. 1441 BC) or late (1290 BC), the Israeli (Israelite) settlement in Mitsrayim would have been in the general vicinity of Tsoan. The Israelis built the store cities of Pitom (Pithom) and Ra’meses, and possibly the latter should be identified with Tsoan. In the account of the exodus in Psalm 78, the city of Tsoan is poetically parallel to Mitsrayim, indicating that it was either the capital or at least a significant city. During the period of Yeshayah (Isaiah), Tsoan was again significant, being designated as the home of the “princes” and “officials” of Mitsrayim (Is 19:11-13; Ez 30:14).
See also Rameses (Place).
ZOAR

One of the “cities of the plain” confederate with Sedom (Sodom), Amorah (Gomorrah), Admah, and Tsevoim (Zeboiim) (Gn 14:2, 8). Tsoar (Zoar), also known by its earlier name Bela, is best known as the town that served as a temporary refuge for Lot and his daughters during the destruction of Sedom and the other cities of the plain (19:22-23, 30). Despite the fact that Tsoar was evidently a small town (v 22; Tsoar means “little”), this place was evidently considered a significant geographical landmark in ancient times. When Avraham (Abraham) and Lot divided the land, Lot selected the land close to Tsoar (13:10). When Mosheh (Moses) surveyed the Promised Land from Mt Pisgah, Tsoar was reckoned as the southern terminus of the plain of the valley of Yeriho (Jericho) (Dt 34:3). During the prophetic period, Tsoar was evidently considered to be on the southern boundary of Moav (Moab) (Is 15:5; Jer 48:4, 34).
See also Cities of the Plain.
ZOBAH

Aramean nation suffering military defeat from Yisrael (Israel) during the early kingdom period. King Sha’ul (Saul) defeated the kings of Tsovah (Zobah) (1 Sm 14:47). Soon after David became king of Yisrael, he defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehov (Rehob), king of Tsovah (2 Sm 8:3-5, 12; 1 Chr 18:3-10; Ps 60 title). Later, the Amonim (Ammonites) hired 20,000 “Aramim (Syrians) of Tsovah” for an anticipated attack by David’s forces. The coalition of Amonim and hired mercenaries was defeated by soldiers led by Yoav (Joab) (2 Sm 10:6-14). When Hadadezer’s army counterattacked, they were again defeated decisively by David (2 Sm 10:15-19; 1 Chr 19:16-19).
ZOBEBAH
One of the sons of Kots (Koz) (or possibly a daughter, since the noun is feminine) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:8). The genealogy is obscure.
ZODIAC*
See Astrology.
ZOHAR
1. Father of Efron (Ephron) the Hiti (Hittite). Avraham (Abraham) bought the cave of Makpelah (Machpelah) from Efron (Gn 23:7-9; 25:9).
2. Alternate spelling of Zerah, Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) son, in Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15. See Zerah #3.
3. Alternate spelling of Yitshar (Izhar) in 1 Chronicles 4:7.
ZOHELETH, Stone of
Alternate rendering for “Serpent’s Stone” in 1 Kings 1:9. See Serpent’s Stone.
ZOHETH
Yishei’s (Ishi’s) son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:20).
ZOPHAH
Helem’s son from Asher’s tribe (1 Chr 7:35-36).
ZOPHAI
Alternate form of Tsuf (Zuph), one of Shmuel’s (Samuel’s) ancestors, in 1 Chronicles 6:26. See Zuph (Person).
ZOPHAR

One of the “counselors” of Iyov (Job) who is listed as a Na’amati (Naamathite) (Jb 2:11; 11:1; 20:1). He offers the most direct accusations against Iyov but later offers sacrifice for Iyov as commanded by the Lord (42:9).
ZOPHIM
Place from which Bil’am (Balaam) pronounced his second blessing upon Yisrael (Israel) (Nm 23:13-16). Tsofim (Zophim) must have been on or near Mt Pisgah.
ZORAH, ZORATHITE

A city of the Shefelah (Shephelah) and its people, attributed to both the tribe of Dan and of Yehudah (Judah) (Jos 15:33; 19:41). It was part of Yehudah’s original allocation but was settled by Danim (Danites) until they established their own territory near Layish (Laish) (Jgs 18:1-11). Originally Tsor’ah (Zorah) and nearby Eshtaol seem to have been settled by residents of Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim) (1 Chr 2:53; 4:2). The city was the home of Manoah, the father of Shimshon (Samson) (Jgs 13:2). Shimshon’s ministry was focused in the region surrounding Tsor’ah and Eshtaol, and he was ultimately buried there. Tsor’ah is traditionally identified with Tell Sur’ah, which is strategically located at the entrance to a large valley leading toward the Mediterranean plain.
ZORITES
Descendants of Salma from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:54). They possibly represent half of the Manahati (Manahathite) clan.
ZOROBABEL*
KJV form of Zerubavel (Zerubbabel), Yerushalem’s (Jerusalem’s) governor after the exile, in Matthew 1:12-13 and Luke 3:27. See Zerubbabel.
ZUAR
Father of Netanel (Nethanel), the leader of Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) tribe at the start of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) wilderness wanderings (Nm 1:8; 2:5; 7:18, 23; 10:15).
ZUPH (Person)

Ancestor of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Shmuel (Samuel) (1 Sm 1:1). Tsuf (Zuph) was a member of the Kohatite (Kohathite) branch of Levites and is listed as the son of Elkanah (different than above) and the father of Toah (1 Chr 6:35). He is the same as Tsuf listed in 1 Chronicles 6:26. It is evident that Tsuf was a Levite, even though he is listed as an Efrati (Ephraimite) in the 1 Samuel passage.
ZUPH (Place)

Place where Sha’ul (Saul) looked for his father’s donkeys prior to his meeting with Shmuel (Samuel) (1 Sm 9:5). It was near the tomb of Rahel (Rachel), which is traditionally placed near the northern border of Benyamin (Benjamin). Tsuf (Zuph) is apparently linked with Shmuel, as one of his ancestors bore the name (see 1 Sm 1:1; 1 Chr 6:35), and his native town was called Ramatayim-Tsofim (Ramathaim-zophim).
ZUR

1. Midyanite (Midianite) prince who was the father of Kozbi (Cozbi), the Midyanite woman who was killed by Pinhas (Phinehas) for consorting with Zimri after the incident at Ba’al-Pe’or (Baal-peor) (Nm 25:15). He was one of the five “kings” of Midyan (Midian) who (with Bil’am (Balaam)) were later killed by the Israelis (Israelites) (31:8). Apparently, he was a vassal of the Amori (Amorite) king Sihon, since he is listed as one of his “princes” (Jos 13:21).
2. Son of Yeiel (Jeiel), the founder of Giveon (Gibeon) (1 Chr 8:30; 9:36). He was a Benyamini (Benjaminite) and a distant relative of Sha’ul (Saul).
ZURIEL
Son of Avihayil (Abihail) and the head of the Merari family of Levites during the wilderness wanderings (Nm 3:35).
ZURISHADDAI
Father of Shelumiel, the leader of Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) tribe at the start of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) wilderness wanderings (Nm 1:6; 2:12; 7:36, 41; 10:19).
ZUZIM*, ZUZITES

One of the kingdoms attacked and defeated by Kedorlaomer’s confederation (Gn 14:5), mentioned as residents of Ham. They were likely located somewhere north of the Arnon River, since the general path of Kedorlaomer was from north to south along the King’s Highway. Possibly these Zuzites are associated with the Zamzumim (Zamzummites) of Deuteronomy 2:20, since both are linked to the same geographical proximity. Furthermore, both passages speak of them in connection with races of giants, including the Horim (Horites), the Emim, and the Refaim (Rephaim).
